There lived in San Franciseo at this time, 1.e.
1909, a Chinese lad fired with a determination to fly,
and though he read with no little apprehension of
Henri Farman's financial failure on Long Island, his
ambition was none the less diminished. This boy, a
youth of twenty Jears, was employed on the staff of THE
WORLD, San Francisco's leading contemporary Chinese
daily•
In 1914, at Canton and other South China cities,
an old Curtiss "Pusher" biplane flown by the illustrious
"Art" Lym, aroused nation-wide interest. He, the
Chinese lad late of San Francisco, had realized his an-
bition to fly, then embarked for China, together with a
youthful understudy named Chan Pon, two second-hand
planes, and an abundance of enthusiasm. He speedily set
about injecting the latter possession into the more ven-
turesome of his countrymen. Lym failed to find flying a
profitable undertaking in the beginning, however, as
those bold enough to desire instruction seldom possessed
the means with which to pay for it. He experienced a
serious setback shortly after his arrival in China when
he wrecked one of the two planes and sustained a broken
leg while making an exhibition flight at Swatow. Never-
theless, success finally arrived, and his future as an
airman was established in China.
One day a part of the fleet anchored in the Pearl

River off Canton revolted, and Lym offered for a con-
sideration to restore peace and order. His offer was
accepted, but not without some skepticism. Since there
were no aerial bombs available, the city was bared of
empty bottles, and these were taken to the airfield and
filled with gasoline and nails, one heaping handful of
nails to each bottle. This ammunition was stowed on
board the plane and Lym took to the air, barely clearing
a row of trees at the windward end, so great was the
load of his craft. He Ilew out over the river, and
after running the gauntlet of a heavy rifle fusilade
from the revolting tars, swooped low over the ships and
rained down a dozen or so missiles on cach. The bottles
burst on striking the decks of the ships and sparks from
the flying nails ignited the gasoline. Iwo ships were
thus set afire and the rebels surrendered forthwith.
Lym, now a hero, returned to the airfield a few minutes
later, and overjoyed with his success and with the large
crowd that had assembled in the meantime to pay him hom-
age, he zoomed wildly & few times low over their heads,
hauled his plane around in a steep bank, then cut his
motor and levelled off for a landing. At about this
point in his maneuvers he doffed helmet and goggles in
recognition of the crowd's wild cheers. The rushing air
filled his eyes with tears, his coat sleeves became en-
tangled with the airleron control yoke and, so the story
continues, the plane completed the first outside loop
accomplished in China. The craft was demolished and Lym
-2-

was rushed to the nearest hospital where he spent the
ensuing three months recovering from shock and from a
badly shattered hip.
"Art" Lym (Lym Fu-Juan)
was born at San Francisco
In 1891, and Learned to fly at North Island in 1913.
At one time he held International Pilot License No. 245.
He is now a Brigadier-General and is second in cornand
of the Canton air force, a corps surpassed in China
only by that of the National Government. Since the
death of Tom Gunn, "Art" Lym 1s reputed to be the old-
est living Chinese aviator in point of service.
